links.note: 471 tells one to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலி, தன்வலி, மாற்றான் வலி, துணைவலி ... தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist with the same closing command, five things to think through until the darkness clears: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன் ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). Read together, 471 measures the parties to a contest and 675 adds the circumstances of the act, and only the deed (வினை) is on both lists.

471 says to weigh one's own strength against the opponent's before acting (தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). 861 states what follows from that weighing when choosing an enemy: avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursue enmity with the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). 861 is 471's comparison turned into a rule.

471 makes comparing strengths the test of whether to act. 250, in the chapter on compassion, uses the same comparison as a brake: when going against those weaker than oneself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), one should think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Being the stronger party permits action in 471, while 250 asks the stronger party to remember what that position feels like from below.

472 says nothing fails for those who know what they can do and what must be known and proceed resting in that (ஒல்வது அறிவது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company and thinking it over themselves (தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்). The promise is the same in both and the condition differs: knowledge of one's own capacity in 472, counsel and deliberation in 462.

472 promises that nothing fails for one who knows his capacity (ஒல்வது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the means and knows the time (அருவினை என்ப உளவோ கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). The chapters on knowing strength and knowing time each make the same claim for their own subject, which suggests each is meant as one necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

594 says gain asks the way and goes to one whose ஊக்கம் does not waver (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான் உழை). 473 says many who did not know their own strength set out on ஊக்கம் and broke midway (வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). The same word names the quality praised in chapter 60 and the cause of failure here, so 473 limits 594: drive pays only when it is matched to a measured strength.

473 says many who did not know their strength broke midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 899 uses the same figure for a king: if those of exalted resolve are angered, even the king breaks midway and loses his kingship (இடைமுரிந்து வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்). Parimelazhagar reads 473 as starting something against those stronger than oneself, and 899 gives one such case, a ruler who misjudges the power of the great.

612 warns against letting a task perish in the middle of doing it (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), because the world gives up on those who leave work unfinished. 473 describes how that happens: people start on enthusiasm without knowing their strength and break midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 612 demands finishing; 473 puts the remedy before the start, in measuring one's strength.

439 commands never to admire oneself (வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை). 474 gives the consequence with the same verb: one who admires himself, without living in accord with others or knowing his measure, perishes quickly (தன்னை வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்). 439 lists self-admiration as a fault to be guarded against, and 474 says what it costs.

474 lists three failings that bring quick ruin: not living in accord (அமைந்தாங்கு ஒழுகான்), not knowing one's measure (அளவறியான்) and admiring oneself. 863 lists the traits of one who is easy for an enemy, and two of them match: he does not know (அறியான்) and does not fit in with others (அமைவிலன்). The chapter on what makes a good enemy to have describes, from the other side, the man 474 says will perish.

474 says the one who admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்) perishes quickly. 978 uses the same phrase to define smallness: greatness always bows, and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In 978 self-admiration is a mark of character, and in 474 it is a miscalculation of strength with a practical result.

475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if too many are piled on (பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும்). 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since there are those who are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி அன்னார்). Both use the axle of a vehicle to say that size misleads: the light thing can break it and the small thing holds it.

475 says a light load breaks the axle when there is too much of it (அப்பண்டம் சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). Parimelazhagar takes the verse as an indirect statement that a strong king who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength when they combine. 873 says this outright: one who, alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more foolish than the mad.

475 says that feathers, light as they are, break an axle when piled too high. 889 says that enmity within, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. Both warn against judging a danger by the smallness of its unit, 475 because small things add up and 889 because of where the small thing sits.

596 says that whatever one thinks of, one should think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்), and that even if this is thwarted it is as if it were not. 476 says that those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and push beyond it (அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின்) end their lives. 596 sets no ceiling on aspiration, while 476 sets one on action: there is a point past which striving higher is fatal.

476 says pushing on past the tip of the branch (இறந்து ஊக்கின்) ends one's life. 858 uses the same verb of hostility: leaning away from it is gain, and if one pushes on to excel in it (மிகல் ஊக்கின்), ruin pushes on in turn (ஊக்குமாம் கேடு). In both, the drive that the book elsewhere praises becomes the cause of ruin when it is carried past a limit.

477 says to give knowing the measure, for that is the way of guarding wealth while bestowing it (அளவறிந்து ஈக அது பொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி). 943 says to eat knowing the measure once the last meal is digested, for that is the way to carry the body far (அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃது உடம்பு பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). The two verses have the same build, a command to know the measure followed by 'that is the way', applied to wealth in one and the body in the other. Both verses are printed with அறவறிந்து in this edition; the reading அளவு is from Parimelazhagar's gloss.

385 says a king is one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion what is guarded (காத்த வகுத்தலும்). 477 gives the rule for the last two of those together: give knowing the measure, and that is the way of guarding wealth while giving it out (பொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி). 385 lists guarding and distributing as separate abilities, and 477 shows them as one act when giving is kept to measure.

512 says the work should go to one who widens the sources of income (வாரி பெருக்கி) and increases the yield. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow (ஆகாறு அளவிட்டிதாயினும்) there is no ruin, as long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக்கடை). 512 values enlarging income, and 478 adds that safety depends on the relation between the two channels and not on the size of the first.

478 says a small income does no harm if spending does not exceed it. 463 says those with understanding do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை ஊக்கார்). Both put keeping what one has ahead of getting more: 478 for the regular flow of income and spending, 463 for a single venture.

479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without a trace (உளபோல இல்லாகித் தோன்றாக் கெடும்). 283 says gain made by theft perishes beyond measure even as it seems to grow (அளவிறந்து ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). Both describe a prosperity whose appearance outlasts its substance, and both tie it to அளவு, which is overstepped by spending in 479 and by stealing in 283.

479 says the life of one who lives without knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) perishes. 947 says that one who eats a great deal without regard to the measure of his digestive fire (தீயளவன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்) gets disease without measure (நோய் அளவின்றிப் படும்). Ignoring a measure brings ruin of wealth in one verse and of health in the other. 479 is printed with a corrupted character in அளவறிந்து in this edition.

220 says that if ruin is said to come through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). 480 says ஒப்புரவு that does not weigh the limit of what one has (உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை) quickly ends one's wealth, and Parimelazhagar draws the lesson that even ஒப்புரவு should not be overdone. The two conflict if 480 is read, with Parimelazhagar, as advice against such giving; if it is read only as a statement of what happens, 220 accepts the same fact and welcomes it.

218 says those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a time without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்). 480 says ஒப்புரவு that does not weigh the limit of one's means (உளவரை தூக்காத) quickly destroys those means. The Book of Virtue praises not letting scarcity stop one's helpfulness, and the Book of Wealth, speaking of a ruler's resources, makes the weighing of means a condition of it.

481 says the crow beats the owl by day (பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை), and Parimelazhagar notes that the owl is the stronger bird. 500 says a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). In both a weaker animal defeats a stronger one through a circumstance, time in 481 and ground in 500, which is how the two adjacent chapters make their cases.

481 says the crow beats the owl by day, so a king who would win needs the right time (வேண்டும் பொழுது). 495 says the crocodile wins in deep water and is killed by others once it leaves the water (புனலின் நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற அடும்). Each verse shows the same creature winning or losing with a change in one condition, time for the owl and place for the crocodile.

482 says that acting in accord with the season (பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) is the rope that keeps fortune from leaving. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (குடிசெய்வார்க்கு இல்லை பருவம்), and that idling and thinking of one's dignity ruins it. The two conflict if பருவம் in 1028 means the right moment for action; Parimelazhagar instead takes it there as seasons of heat, rain and cold used as an excuse to put work off, which removes the conflict.

482 pictures fortune (திரு) as something that leaves unless tied, and names timely action as the rope (தீராமை ஆர்க்கும் கயிறு). 617 pictures her as living in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்), with her dark elder sister living in sloth. Both treat fortune as a visitor kept by conduct, and they name different conduct: timing in 482, steady effort in 617.

483 asks whether any deed is hard for one who acts with the means and knows the time (அருவினை என்ப உளவோ கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 631 defines a minister as one who excels in means, time, method and the hard deed itself (கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும் அருவினையும்). The same three words, கருவி, காலம் and அருவினை, appear in both, so the minister of 631 is the person in whom 483's condition is met.

483 asks whether anything is hard if one acts with the means and at the right time. 537 says there is nothing that cannot be done on the ground that it is hard, if one acts with the tool of unforgetting care (அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை பொச்சாவாக் கருவியால்). 537 uses 483's word கருவி as a figure, making attention itself one of the means that remove difficulty.

483 names two conditions that make a hard deed possible, means and time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன்). 675 keeps 483's pair and sets it inside a fuller list.

484 says that even if one has the world in mind, it comes to hand when one considers the time and acts by the place (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும் காலம் கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்). 485 reverses the same words: those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, considering the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது ஞாலம் கருதுபவர்). 484 states the condition for acting and 485 its other side, that until the time comes the ambitious do not move.

484 says the world comes to hand if one considers the time and acts by the place (இடத்தாற் செயின்). 497, in the next chapter, uses the same phrase: one needs no support but fearlessness if one thinks everything through and acts by the place (எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்). 484 names place as a second condition beside time, and the following chapter, with 497, takes it up as its own subject.

484 says a king who considers time and place can gain even the world (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும்). 610 says a king without sloth gains at once all the expanse crossed by the one who measured with his foot (மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான் தாஅயதெல்லாம்). Both promise the whole earth, one to timing and the other to unremitting effort, so the two chapters make the same claim for different qualities.

485 says those who aim at the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது). 672 says to take one's time over what should be done slowly (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால) and not to delay what should be done without delay. Both treat waiting as a decision that fits some tasks, and 672 adds the second half that 485 leaves out.

485 praises waiting for the right time. 671 says deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (அத்துணிவு தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 671 marks the limit of 485: waiting that is fixed on the time (காலம் கருதி) is part of the plan, and holding back after the decision, for no such reason, is a fault.

486 says the holding back of a person of energy is like a fighting ram stepping back in order to charge (பொருதகர் தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து). 827 says not to trust humble words from an enemy, because the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both use a drawing back that comes before a blow: 486 recommends it to oneself, and 827 teaches one to see it in an opponent.

152 says always to bear with an excess done to one, and that forgetting it is better still (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம் பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). Both hold back the outward response, and they differ on what happens inside: 152 wants the wrong forgotten, 487 wants the anger kept. The conflict holds if both are read as general advice; 152 belongs to the householder's virtues and Parimelazhagar takes 487 as addressed to kings facing enemies.

309 says that if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி), everything one has thought of is gained at once. 487 says the bright keep their anger within (உள்வேர்ப்பர்) while they watch for the time. Each ties success to what is done with anger inside, and they say opposite things. Parimelazhagar restricts 309 to the ascetic and 487 to kings, so the conflict depends on reading both as addressed to anyone.

301 says that the one who truly guards against anger guards it where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்); where it cannot, guarding or not makes no difference. 487 has the bright hold back anger now, when showing it would not serve, and keep it inside for the right time. On the reading that 487's anger is to be released when it can succeed, it describes the restraint that 301 says does not count, and withholds the one that does.

488 says to bear with enemies on seeing them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), and that when their end comes the head goes down; Parimelazhagar glosses the first command as bowing to them. 828 warns that a weapon lies hidden inside an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்). Both take a show of submission between enemies to be a tactic: 488 advises it for oneself, and 828 warns that the other side does the same.

488 says to bear with enemies until their end comes (இறுவரை காணின்). 879 says to cut down a thorn tree while it is young, because once it has hardened it destroys the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து). 879 limits 488's patience: waiting serves when time works against the enemy, and not when the enemy is growing stronger.

151 says that bearing with those who scorn one, as the earth holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போல), is the highest thing. 488 uses a verb of carrying for the same act, bearing with those who would harm one (சுமக்க), and makes it a means: one bears them until their end comes and their head goes down. The two conflict if both are read as answers to how one should treat those who wrong one, since forbearance is the goal in 151 and a way to the enemy's fall in 488. 151 is addressed to the householder and 488 to a king, which is the other way to read them.

489 says that when what is hard to get has come, one should at that very point do what is hard to do (இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, and that on getting it one should at once do what stays (அதுபெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both reason from something that will not last, an opportunity in 489 and wealth in 333, to acting at once, and 333 turns the king's rule of timing toward lasting good.

26 says the great are those who do what is hard to do, and the small are those who cannot (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 489 uses the same phrase and adds a condition of time: hard deeds are to be done at the moment a rare opportunity arrives (செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 26 places the ability in the person; 489 says it also depends on a moment that is itself hard to come by (எய்தற்கரியது).

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து), and like its strike when the moment is right. 126 says that one who can draw in the five senses like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) in one birth has protection for seven. Both teach restraint through an animal that draws itself in. The tortoise's withdrawal is the discipline itself, and the heron's is half of a pair that ends in a strike (குத்து).

490 holds up the heron, which stays still until the moment and then strikes, as a model for acting on enemies. 274 says that doing wrong under cover of austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds (புதல்மறைந்து வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று). The pattern of stillness that hides a coming strike is the same in both. It is recommended to the king waiting for his time, and it is the figure of fraud in one who wears the ascetic's appearance.
